title: The Race Car Ford’s Building for Le Mans Is “95 Percent” Complete, and It Has a Name

body_markdown:
It’s no secret that Ford is building a new car to take on the top class of the backbreaking 24 Hours of Le Mans endurance race in 2027. We’re pleased to report that after a sneak peek, the car looks good and sounds even better. We also learned its name: GT41.


If that sounds like a reference to the GT40 and its famous, overall 1-2-3 victory at Le Mans in ’66, retold by the movie[Ford v Ferrari](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/ford-v-ferrari-is-tense-timely-transcendent/) in 2019, of course it is. Ford is very happy if you made the connection, because its new ad campaign, called “Go Like Hell,” is designed to drive home that very message.


But neither that impressive debut commercial, voiced by Matt Damon (who played Carroll Shelby in *Ford v Ferrari* ) and directed by Zack Snyder (famous for *300* , *Man of Steel* , and “The Snyder Cut” of *Justice League* ), nor the in-person reveal of the car at Ford Field in Detroit during the Lions game on Thanksgiving Day, means much without hearing from the team that’s currently testing the race car.


If you keep up with sports-car racing, you know that Ford’s 2016 Le Mans win, on the anniversary of its 1966 victory there, was in class, not overall. This time, the GT41 is aimed at an overall win.


And you may also be aware that Ford is building this car on a very tight deadline. Engineering a new race car typically takes a bare minimum of two to three years; Ford is trying to do it 18 months. You may also know that the 2027 World Endurance Championship (WEC) season, of which the 24 Hours of Le Mans is the crown jewel, does not start in June in France, but in March in Qatar. Ford is fielding a two-car lineup for 2027, and plans to take part in all nine rounds.


[Cameron Neveu](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/cameron-neveu/)


[Cameron Neveu](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/cameron-neveu/)


[Cameron Neveu](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/cameron-neveu/)


[Cameron Neveu](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/cameron-neveu/)


Gutsy, right? At this point in the testing phase, says program head Dan Sayers, “We haven’t got time to have issues that take more than a week to solve.” The pressure on him and the team makes his calm, cheerful demeanor even more impressive: With the homologation process just weeks away, “We’re 95 percent of the way there on the specification of the car.” That said, it’s hardly his first rodeo: A veteran of Aston Martin’s sports car programs, he led design and development for the V12 Vantage race car. Before his current role spearheading Ford Racing’s Hypercar program, he was program director at Rd Bull Ford Powertrains, working on the 2026 F1 power unit program. You know, chill stuff.


He’s fresh off the GT41’s first 30-hour endurance test, held at the 3.2-mile MotorLand Aragón in Alcañiz, Spain. In the prior five tests,[held at tracks across Europe](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/ford-hypercar-completes-its-first-on-track-test/) , the car had only run “about a stint and a half” continuously.


“It was quite a leap into the unknown,” Sayers says, because the team was also testing an updated specification of the 5.4-liter, naturally-aspirated V-8, with more power and reduced mass—”which is obviously music to our ears”—but it had only 30 hours of dyno time and no on-track time.


“Slight risk, I would say, ” says Sayers. “I’m fairly risk-averse, but \[it was a\] slight risk putting \[the new specification of engine\] straight into the car and going for 30 hours rather than doing a test beforehand. But that’s what a condensed test program does.”


Fortunately, he’s had help on the hybrid system with Ford employees embedded with F1 partner Red Bull. “Whilst they haven’t been able to port \[that knowledge\] across as such, they’ve learned a huge amount in the last couple of years, which is directly influencing and helping our program.”


[Cameron Neveu](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/cameron-neveu/)


The team took two cars to MotorLand. Only one attempted the 30-hour test; the other was a test bed for controls development—a simple phrase that hides massive complexity. “They’ll keep being developed until we stop running the car,” Sayers says. Because of that, his primary focus at MotorLand was the endurance car. And how did it do? It needed an unscheduled engine change at 2:30 in the morning, due to a cooling system issue—all the more frustrating because the issue was a simple one—and that was all. Sayers is pleased.


“Was MotorLand ever going to be a plain-sailing, 30-hour test, no faults, no issues? Of course not. No one thought it would be, but to come out of that with over 24 hours of running and no problems that aren’t relatively simple to solve is probably the best we could hope for.”


Dan Sayers, thinking about race cars.


Ford Racing


Why MotorLand? It replicates the high top speeds they’ll see at Le Mans without testing at Le Mans, which is impossible apart from race week, because part of the circuit is comprised of public roads. Top speed isn’t the only quality that makes Aragon or Le Mans challenging, of course: The intense braking zones immediately following are key for understanding how the car brakes, and the sustained speeds reveal how your aerodynamic package performs. They aren’t simply testing in-person every two weeks: “We’re fortunate to have a dedicated homologation wind tunnel car that’s based in America,” says Sayers. “So we are updating that car each time we go into the tunnel with things we’ve learned from the track. And then vice versa.”


[Cameron Neveu](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/cameron-neveu/)


[Cameron Neveu](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/cameron-neveu/)


The MotorLand test was also the first where all seven drivers were present, a group that now includes reserve driver and two-time Le Mans class winner Tom Dillmann. Unfortunately, says Sayers, Logan Sargeant and Mike Rockenfeller were both sick; the former couldn’t drive and the latter did only “a couple of runs.”


That group also includes Matt Campbell, Sebastian Priaulx, Tom Blomqvist and Nick Yelloly (who shared a car with Dillmann for his two LMP2 wins in ’25 and ’26). Blomqvist and Yelloly competed in the WEC’s North American counterpart, the IMSA WeatherTech SportsCar Championship, with Acura last season. Priaulx raced Mustangs in IMSA and in WEC last year, and Matt Campbell won the IMSA GTP championship with Porsche Penske Motorsport.


U.S. racing fans eager to hear whether Ford is planning to enter the GT41 in IMSA competition will have to wait, because although such an entry seems likely, Ford hasn’t announced anything, and it’s way too late to plan for 2027, as IMSA’s season starts in January with the Rolex 24 Hours at Daytona.


[Cameron Neveu](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/cameron-neveu/)


[Cameron Neveu](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/cameron-neveu/)


Watching the team begin to gel in recent months is a point of pride for Sayers. “To see the car come together is one thing, but I think to see the team come together over the last probably two, three months has been really rewarding.” With the European testing done, the team will pack up and ship the cars to the U.S. to test at tracks across North America.


They have their work cut out for them, but if he’s nervous, Sayers doesn’t show it. You wouldn’t really expect him to, either, given his extensive experience in motorsports. He spent 10 years at Prodrive overseeing Aston Martin’s GT4 and then GT3 programs, then spent five years as technical director for all Aston Martin Racing. He’s got a Le Mans class win under his belt, too: GTE-Pro in 2017 with the Vantage GTE. “We know what we’ve got to do,” says Sayers, who describes his job as alleviating the “pressure cooker” effect on his people. “We know we’ve got to focus on ourselves and our execution.”


Though the 2027 WEC season kicks off with a test, then a race in Qatar in March, the real test of Ford’s mettle will be that fifth round, held the second weekend of June at the 24 Hours of Le Mans. There the two GT41s will compete for the overall win in the Hypercar class against Alpine, Aston Martin, BMW, Toyota, Ferrari, Genesis, Cadillac, and[fellow newcomer McLaren](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/meet-mclarens-hypercar-challenger/) . But as race fans know, the real competition isn’t the other cars on the grid, or the other teams in the tiny garages: It’s Le Mans itself.


[Cameron Neveu](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/cameron-neveu/)
